meta.blurb: A cabin ten feet by fifteen, three chairs, a field of beans and a quiet pond. Henry David Thoreau moved in on 4 July 1845 to find out how little a person needs, and how much a single day can hold.
meta.bible: Henry David Thoreau: American writer and thinker, born in Concord, Massachusetts; he published Walden in 1854, after living at the pond from 4 July 1845 to 6 September 1847. Walden Pond: the clear, deep pond in the woods near Concord, where he built his Cabin on land belonging to his friend Ralph Waldo Emerson. Concord: the town in Massachusetts. Emerson: writer and neighbour who owned the land. The cabin: about ten feet by fifteen, built from pine trees he cut himself and boards from an old shanty, with a Chimney, a Fireplace and a Garden. Homer: ancient Greek poet; Thoreau kept the Iliad on his table. Alek Therien: a French-Canadian woodchopper who visited. Beans: he planted a bean-field of about two and a half acres. Flint's Pond: another pond nearby. Baker Farm: a farm where he met an Irish labourer, John Field. Fitchburg Railroad: the railway that passed near the pond. Ganges: the great river of India. Key terms: Loon, Hare, Squirrel, Owl, Partridge, Woodchopper, Shanty, Ice, Thaw, Huckleberries, Sandbank, Poll tax, Constable, Laundry. Voice and tone: calm, thoughtful and curious, with gentle humour; a year-by-year walk through the seasons; claims about money and time are Thoreau's own opinions, stated as his.

B1B2: In 1845 a young writer named Henry David Thoreau left the town of Concord, in Massachusetts. He wanted to live alone in the woods beside Walden Pond.
Thoreau did not go to the woods to hide from people. He wanted to live carefully, face the basic facts of life, and learn what life had to teach him.
Thoreau saw that many of his neighbours worked all their lives to pay for farms and houses. To him they seemed more like slaves to their possessions than free people.
Thoreau asked what a person really needs to live. His answer was short: food, a place to live, clothing and fuel for a fire.
Thoreau believed that clothes and houses should be useful, not fashionable. He thought it was foolish to be more afraid of a patch than of a lack of honesty.
Thoreau said the real cost of anything is the amount of life that we must spend to get it. A thing that takes years of work may be too expensive.
In the spring he borrowed an axe from a friend and went to the woods. He cut down tall pine trees to make the frame of his little house.
Thoreau bought the boards of an old shanty for a few dollars. Some friends then came to help him lift the wooden frame of the new house.
The cabin was about ten feet wide and fifteen feet long, with a window and a door. Before winter he built a chimney of old bricks, and the whole house cost very little.
On 4 July 1845, Independence Day in America, Thoreau moved into the cabin. He liked the idea of beginning his own independent life on that day.
Thoreau kept careful accounts of everything that he spent in a year. He said that by working only about six weeks a year, he could pay for everything he needed.
Thoreau loved the morning, and he began each day with a bath in the pond. For him, morning was not a time of day but a state of mind.
Thoreau said that our lives are wasted by too many small things. He believed we should keep things simple, and then simplify them again.
A railroad ran close to the pond, and Thoreau liked to watch the trains. He thought that people could easily become servants of such machines, instead of using them well.
Thoreau loved to read, and he kept a copy of Homer's Iliad on his table. He read a little in the mornings when he had time.
Thoreau said that good books must be read with effort and care. Yet he also thought that nature was a kind of book, and he spent many hours reading it.
In the evening, Thoreau sat at his door and listened. He heard the church bells of Concord, the whistle of the train, and the call of owls in the dark.
Thoreau lived alone, yet he said he was seldom lonely. He found good company in the woods, the pond, the weather, and his own thoughts.
Thoreau kept three chairs in his very small wooden cabin. One was for solitude, two were for friendship, and three were for company.
One of Thoreau's most welcome visitors was a French-Canadian woodchopper named Alek Therien. He was strong, cheerful and wise in his own simple way.
Other visitors came as well, including children, travellers and curious neighbours. Some came for berries, and some only wanted to see how he lived.
Thoreau planted about two and a half acres of beans, along with potatoes and corn. He wanted to grow some of his own food and sell a little.
Each morning Thoreau went out to hoe his beans. He joked that he was making the earth speak beans instead of weeds, and he enjoyed the quiet work.
The beans did not make Thoreau rich, and he earned only a small profit. Still, he felt that he had learned useful lessons about work, patience, and the earth.
Thoreau walked to the village of Concord every day or two. He liked to hear the news and the gossip, much as one enjoys the song of birds.
In July 1846 a constable stopped Thoreau in the village. He had refused to pay a poll tax, and so he spent one night in the town jail.
Someone else paid the tax, and Thoreau was freed the next morning. He then went straight to pick huckleberries with a group of friends.
Thoreau describes Walden Pond with great love and care. It is deep and clear, and its colour changes from blue to green depending on the sky and the light.
Some neighbours said that the pond had no bottom. In winter Thoreau measured it through the ice and found that its deepest part was about a hundred feet.
Thoreau also visited the other ponds near Concord, such as Flint's Pond. He enjoyed them all, but he thought Walden was the most beautiful.
One rainy day Thoreau took shelter at Baker Farm and met a poor Irish labourer named John Field. He thought John Field could be happier with a simpler life.
Thoreau used to fish and hunt, but in the woods he felt less and less wish to do so. He believed that people grow better by learning to control their desires.
A wild mouse lived under Thoreau's cabin and grew very tame. It ran up his clothes and even ate a piece of cheese from his fingers.
One day Thoreau saw a great battle between red ants and black ants. The tiny creatures fought as fiercely as soldiers, and he watched them for hours.
A loon, a large water bird, lived on the pond. Thoreau tried to follow it in his boat, but the loon always came up far away and laughed at him.
As autumn arrived, Thoreau gathered nuts and wild grapes. He finished the chimney and put plaster on the walls to keep out the winter cold.
Thoreau collected dry wood from the forest to burn in his fireplace. He found that a warm fire and a good book were among the greatest pleasures of life.
Long ago, other people had lived in the woods near the pond. Their houses were gone, and only holes in the ground and a few old stones remained.
In winter the woods were covered with deep snow, and very few people visited the cabin. Thoreau enjoyed the quiet days and long evenings by the fire.
In winter Thoreau watched the animals around his cabin. He saw squirrels, foxes, hares and owls, and he often left scraps of food out for them.
In winter Thoreau cut a hole in the ice and looked into the pond. Below the ice, the water was calm and clear, and he could see the fish swimming.
One winter, many men came with saws and horses to cut ice from the pond. They loaded the large blocks onto sledges and took them away to be shipped.
Thoreau often thought about the far places where the ice would go. He imagined that the pure water of Walden might one day mix with the sacred water of the Ganges.
In spring the thick ice on the pond began to melt away. The pond made loud booming and cracking sounds as the ice broke up, and Thoreau listened with great delight.
On a railway bank, melting sand and clay flowed out in shapes like leaves and branches. Thoreau thought it was a wonderful sight, as though the earth were alive.
In spring the birds came back to the woods, and small green plants began to grow. Thoreau heard the first sparrow and the first robin, and he was very happy.
One evening Thoreau saw wild geese flying north over the pond. Their loud calls told him that spring had truly come, and he felt full of hope.
On 6 September 1847, after two years in the woods, Thoreau left his cabin. He said that he had several more lives to live and could not spend more time on this one.
Thoreau's experiment taught him one important thing about life. If a person goes confidently in the direction of his dreams, he said, he will meet with success he did not expect.
The book ends with a very short and surprising story. A bug hatches from an old table of apple wood after many years, and Thoreau says that it shows that new life is always possible.
C1C2: In the spring of 1845, Henry David Thoreau, a young writer from Concord in Massachusetts, decided to try an unusual experiment. He would leave the town and live by himself in the woods beside Walden Pond, supporting himself by the work of his own hands. His friend Ralph Waldo Emerson owned the land, and he gave Thoreau permission to build there.

Thoreau tells us plainly that he did not go to the woods in order to escape the world but to see it more clearly. He wished to live deliberately, to face only the essential facts of life, and to discover whether it had something to teach him before it was too late. He feared that, when he came to die, he would find that he had never really lived.

Looking around Concord, Thoreau saw neighbours who laboured from dawn to dusk to pay for farms, barns and tools that seemed to own them rather than serve them. Many had inherited their troubles, he thought, and carried them through life as if they were heavy loads on their backs. It troubled him that so few of them had the leisure to ask whether all that work was necessary.

To find out what was truly necessary, Thoreau reduced the question to its simplest terms and asked what a person needs in order to stay alive and warm. His list was very short, and it contained only food, shelter, clothing and fuel. Everything else, he suggested, was either a luxury or a burden, and many people gave up years of life in pursuit of the extras.

Thoreau had little patience for fashion, and he believed that clothing should be chosen for warmth and honest wear rather than for show. He pointed out that people seemed more afraid of a patch on a coat than of a flaw in their own conduct. A sound old garment, mended with care, was in his opinion nothing to be ashamed of.

Thoreau offered a measure of price that few merchants would recognise: the cost of a thing, he said, is the amount of life that must be spent in getting it, now or in the end. By this reckoning, a handsome house that requires thirty years of labour to pay for may be dearer than it looks. He invited his readers to do the arithmetic honestly, and to ask whether the price they paid was really worth it.

Early in 1845, Thoreau borrowed an axe, walked to the pine woods beside the pond and began to cut the timbers for his house. It was pleasant work in the fresh spring air, and he never hurried, pausing often to enjoy the birds and the smell of the freshly cut wood. When the work was done, he returned the axe to its owner a little sharper than he had received it, which pleased him.

For the walls, Thoreau bought the boards of a rough old shanty belonging to a railway worker, paying only a few dollars for them. He took the boards apart, laid them out in the sun to dry and then, with the help of several friends, raised the frame of the little house. It was, he said, more a pleasant gathering of neighbours than a day of hard labour, and the work was soon done.

The finished cabin measured about ten feet by fifteen, with a door, a window or two, a small attic and a cellar beneath the floor. It cost only a few dozen dollars in materials, as Thoreau was fond of pointing out, which he said was less than the yearly rent of a student's room at a college. Later, before the cold arrived, he built a chimney of old bricks, and the little house was ready for its first winter.

On the fourth of July, 1845, which is Independence Day in America, Thoreau carried his few belongings into the cabin and made it his home. He enjoyed the thought that he was beginning his own small experiment in independence on the same day that his country celebrated its own. The house was unfinished, with no chimney and no plaster, but he was free.

Thoreau kept careful accounts of his spending, and he reported with satisfaction that by working only about six weeks a year he could meet all the expenses of living. This left him the remainder of the year, he said, free for study, walking and thought. Whether others could do the same is open to debate, but he offered his figures as a challenge to the reader.

Thoreau treasured the early hours, and he began each day by bathing in the clear water of the pond, which he regarded as a kind of daily religious exercise. Morning, he said, is when there is a dawn in us, and the day truly begins only when we are awake in mind as well as in body. Most of the people he knew, he thought, were still half asleep at noon.

Our lives, Thoreau complained, are frittered away by detail, and a person would do well to keep his affairs to two or three instead of a hundred or a thousand. His advice, repeated almost like a chant, was to simplify, simplify, simplify, until nothing remained that was not truly needed. A life stripped of its unnecessary business, he believed, leaves much more room for the few things that really matter.

A railway line ran along the western shore of the pond, and the passing trains were a daily reminder of the busy world that Thoreau had left behind. He did not hate the railway, but he suspected that people were often in more danger of becoming the servants of their inventions than of benefiting from them. We do not ride on the railroad, he quipped, for it rides upon us.

Though he had little time for newspapers, Thoreau loved the great books of the past, and he kept a copy of Homer's Iliad on his table, reading it in the original Greek whenever he could. Such works, he believed, were written by people who thought with care, and they deserved to be read with the same care. Reading of this kind, he said, is a labour and not a pastime, and it asks for the same training that an athlete gives his body.

Thoreau knew that books could carry the best thoughts of the past, yet he warned his readers not to forget the wider book that lay outside the cabin door. The pond, the trees and the changing sky were also texts to be read, he thought, and an hour spent watching them could teach as much as an hour spent in the library. The best education, in his opinion, used both of them, and the person who read only one of them would always be half-taught.

Sitting at his door in the evening, Thoreau listened to an orchestra of sounds. There were the church bells of Concord drifting across the fields, the whistle of the distant train and, after dark, the hoots of owls and the sad song of the whip-poor-will. He found that each of them made the woods seem more alive, and he never felt that the silence around him was empty.

Thoreau lived alone, and yet he reported, with a certain pride, that he was almost never lonely, because the woods, the pond and the weather made excellent companions. Solitude, he argued, is not measured in miles from other people, and a scholar in a crowded city may be lonelier than a farmer in an empty field. In the end he came to think of the quiet of the woods as a kind of friend, always willing to keep him company.

In his small cabin, Thoreau kept three chairs, and he liked to say that one was for solitude, two for friendship and three for society. When more visitors arrived, they simply stood, and he found that a small house encouraged people to stand close together and speak softly. Even in a place so small, he noted with amusement, there was always room for good conversation.

Among the most frequent visitors to the cabin was Alek Therien, a French-Canadian woodchopper, who was strong, cheerful and apparently content with very little. He had little schooling, but he carried a fund of shrewd sense and an easy laugh, and he found a great deal to enjoy in the day's work. Thoreau admired him as a man who was thoroughly at home in the world.

Many others found their way to the cabin: children gathering berries, farmers curious about his experiment and wandering travellers who simply wanted to rest. Thoreau received them with cheerful courtesy, though he admitted that he sometimes preferred the visitors who were content to say little. A quiet guest, he thought, was among life's rarest and most pleasant gifts, and he was always grateful to meet one.

In the early summer, Thoreau cleared a patch of land near the cabin and planted it with beans, together with smaller amounts of potatoes, corn and peas. The field covered about two and a half acres, and he hoped to grow some of his own food and to sell the extra for a little money. It was not much land, but it was enough to keep him busy every morning.

Each morning Thoreau hoed his beans, wetting the plants with the dew and enjoying the rhythm of the work, though he admitted that he was waging a war on weeds that seemed to be endless. He joked that he was making the earth say beans instead of grass, and the thought amused him. The work was hard, but it brought a close knowledge of the ground beneath his feet.

The harvest brought Thoreau only a small profit, but he did not count it a failure, for the real return, he felt, came in the form of lessons about patience, labour and the earth. He had learned how to read the weather and how to value a simple meal that he had grown himself. Even a modest field, he concluded, can be an education, and he felt that he had been well taught by his beans.

Every day or two, Thoreau walked the short distance into Concord to hear the gossip and the news, which he found as refreshing in its way as the rustling of leaves or the chatter of squirrels. He enjoyed the life of the village, but he never quite felt that he belonged to it, and he did not wish to. Each time he returned, he felt grateful for the quiet of his own woods.

In July 1846, as Thoreau walked into the village to collect a shoe from the mender, a constable arrested him for refusing to pay a poll tax. He had declined, he said, because he did not wish to support a government that allowed slavery. He spent a single night in the town jail, and the experience stayed with him for the rest of his life.

The next morning, someone else paid the tax on his behalf, and Thoreau was released, a little annoyed to find that his small protest had been undone. He collected his mended shoe and joined a party that was going out to pick huckleberries on a nearby hill. By the time he reached the hilltop, he wrote, the state was nowhere to be seen.

Thoreau describes Walden Pond with evident affection, calling it a clear and deep body of water whose colour varies from blue to green according to the sky and the angle of the sunlight. Held in a basin of sand and stone, with no stream flowing into it, it seemed to him a kind of earth's eye, and he never tired of looking into it. In clear weather, he could see down to the stones on the bottom, a long way below the surface.

Local people liked to say that Walden Pond had no bottom, but Thoreau, who also worked as a surveyor, saw no reason to accept the story without proof. Using a long line and a heavy stone, he measured the pond through the winter ice and found its deepest part to be a little over a hundred feet. He also made a careful map of the whole pond, and with this honest piece of work the old legend was finished for good.

Thoreau explored the other ponds of the neighbourhood, including the larger Flint's Pond, and he described each one with care. He admired their different shapes and colours, yet he returned to Walden as the most beautiful of them all, particularly for the clearness of its water and the wildness of its shores. A place, he implied, becomes dear to us only by being familiar, and he had walked those shores until he knew them like his own hand.

One rainy afternoon, Thoreau took shelter at Baker Farm, where he met John Field, an Irish labourer who worked hard to support a large family. He felt sorry for the household's troubles and told them that they might live better if they lived more simply, but Field could not believe it. The visit left Thoreau thoughtful about how hard it is to change another person's way of life.

As a boy, Thoreau had hunted and fished like his neighbours, but in the quiet of the woods he found that the wish to do so was slowly fading. He believed that every person has both a wild and a spiritual side, and that the nobler of the two is cultivated by patient self-discipline. These were deeply personal convictions, offered not as rules but as his own experience.

A wild mouse that had made its nest beneath the cabin gradually grew so tame that it would run across the floor and eat crumbs near his feet. In time it climbed his clothes and sat on his hand, eating a piece of cheese from his very fingers. Thoreau was delighted by this small friendship, which he counted among the pleasures of his solitary life.

One day, near his woodpile, Thoreau came upon a battle between red ants and black ants, and he settled down to watch the whole contest with a scholar's absorption. The tiny creatures fought with as much determination as any human armies, and he described the scene in the grand language of epic poetry. The mock heroics were, perhaps, his way of gently smiling at the wars that human beings are so quick to fight.

A loon, which is a large diving bird, visited the pond in the autumn, and Thoreau set out in his boat to see whether he could follow it. Each time the bird dived, it reappeared at a distance he had not expected, and it seemed to mock him with its wild, laughing cry. After a long game, he admitted that the loon was by far the better player.

With the arrival of autumn, Thoreau gathered chestnuts and wild grapes, set about finishing his chimney of old bricks and plastered the inside walls of the cabin to keep out the cold. The work was slow, and the days were growing short, but he laboured on until the house felt warm and secure. He took great pleasure in a shelter that he had made himself, and he did not envy anyone living in a grander house.

Through the autumn and winter, Thoreau gathered fallen branches and old stumps from the woods and stacked them near the cabin for burning. He found that the fire gave him a double warmth, first when he gathered the wood and again when he burned it. A bright hearth and a good book, he thought, were rich pleasures that cost almost nothing.

As he walked in the woods, Thoreau came across the sites of cottages where other people had once lived, including some who had been freed from slavery and had settled in these hills. Of their homes, only hollows in the ground and the remains of chimneys were left, and he wondered who they were and what they had hoped for. The earth, it seemed, forgets very quickly, and a whole household can vanish from a hillside within a few short years.

When winter closed in, the woods lay under a deep covering of snow, and the few visitors who braved the cold stayed only a short time. Thoreau found the long quiet evenings by the fire agreeable, and he felt very much at home in his small house, with the wind outside and the warmth within. Winter, he thought, was a good season for thinking, and he used its quiet as other people use a library.

The woods in winter were far from empty, and Thoreau enjoyed watching the red squirrels, the foxes, the hares and the partridges that came to his door. He scattered corn and scraps for them, and heard owls at night, hooting from the dark pines. The animals, he found, were cheerful neighbours, and they made the snowy season feel full of life.

On winter mornings, Thoreau cut a hole in the thick ice and looked down into the pond, where the water lay dark, calm and surprisingly clear. Through it he fished, took his soundings and watched the pale light that filtered down into a hidden world. He found that the pond, which seemed frozen and dead from above, was still quietly alive below.

One winter, a crew of men arrived with horses, sledges and long saws to harvest the pond's ice, which they cut into huge blocks and piled in great stacks by the shore. It was to be shipped to distant cities, where it would be used to keep food and drinks cool in summer. Thoreau watched with a mixture of curiosity and regret at this intrusion into his private pond.

Thoreau liked to imagine the long journey that the pond's ice might take, across oceans and through harbours, to ports as far away as India. He pictured the pure water of Walden mingling with the sacred waters of the Ganges, and it pleased him to think that his small pond was joined to the great rivers of the world. A quiet place, he felt, is never truly alone, for it is joined to the whole world by water, wind and the long travels of its ice.

As the days lengthened, the ice began to melt, and the whole pond boomed and cracked with a sound like distant thunder as the sheet gave way. Thoreau listened with delight, for it told him that winter's grip was loosening and that the long-awaited thaw had come. The final breaking of the ice, he wrote, was a kind of annual celebration.

At a deep cutting beside the railway, Thoreau watched the thawing sandbank send down streams of sand and clay that spread into patterns like leaves, veins and branches. He was filled with wonder, for it seemed to him as though he were looking at the earth in the very act of creation, still being shaped and still alive. Nature, he decided, was a restless artist, forever beginning again, and he was happy to be there to watch the work.

With spring came the return of the birds: the bluebird, the sparrow and the robin were heard one after the other, and the first green grass pushed through the thawing ground. Thoreau welcomed each as an old friend, and the whole landscape seemed to be waking from a long sleep. The change from brown to green, he wrote, was like a miracle repeated every year.

One spring evening, Thoreau heard the honking of wild geese and looked up to see a long line of them flying north above the pond. Their strong calls, ringing across the water, told him more clearly than any calendar that the winter was over and that the world was beginning again. He felt his own spirits rise with them, as if he too were setting out on a journey.

On the sixth of September, 1847, after two years, two months and two days beside the pond, Thoreau closed the cabin door and returned to the village. He departed, he explained, for as good a reason as had drawn him there, since he perceived that he had several more lives to live and could spare no further time for that one. It was time, he felt, to move on, and he never spoke of the choice with any regret.

Thoreau's experiment left him with a simple conviction: if a person advances confidently in the direction of his dreams and endeavours to live the life he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours. The lesson was a simple one, but it was won by two years of quiet living. He never told others to copy him, but urged each of them to find a way of their own.

Thoreau closes his book with a story of a strong and beautiful insect that emerged, after many years, from the dry wood of an old apple-tree table, having been sealed inside the tree long before. To him it was a symbol that life can awaken at any time, in any person, however long it has lain dormant. Only that day dawns, he concludes, to which we are awake, and the sun is but a morning star.
